$authoring: THE authored source of every design value in this package. Nothing else in
packages/gl-charts may author a hex, size, width or opacity.
`grammar.md` at the repo root is the source of truth; this file is its
machine-readable encoding for the web / SVG medium. Change a value in
`grammar.md` first, then here, then run `node scripts/emit-tokens.mjs`.
`node scripts/check-tokens.mjs` re-parses grammar.md's colour tables and
fails if the two disagree.
Shape:
meta          file headers + prose that outlived the code it documented
declarations  ordered list; one per export in src/tokens.ts
css           the ordered `.gl-figure` custom-property block (src/tokens.css);
rows REFERENCE declaration entries, so no value is authored twice
downstream    the propagation table `check-tokens.mjs --downstream` scans
Declaration kinds: map · tone · tones · list · ramps · scalar · derived ·
roles · interface · type · aggregate. Every declaration and entry may carry
`doc` (string or array of lines) — that prose is emitted as JSDoc / CSS
comments and is the most valuable thing in this file: it records WHICH spec
rule the value serves and what breaks without it.
`css` on an entry names the custom property (which differs from the TS name:
`ink[2]` → `--ink-2`) plus any spec-PDF aliases (`--chart-axis-label`).
`grammar` on a declaration says how check-tokens verifies it.

tsHeader: GL chart design tokens — web / SVG medium.
DOWNSTREAM COPY. `grammar.md` at the repo root is the source of truth for
every value in this file. If a value here disagrees with `grammar.md`, this
file is the bug. Change the token in `grammar.md` first, then in
`tokens.json`, then re-emit and update every other downstream encoding
listed in README.md ("Where each value lives downstream").
Units: the spec is written in CSS px, and this is the web medium, so every
size converts 1:1 — no scaling table is needed here (contrast `theme_gl.R`,
which has to convert px → pt → ggplot linewidth).
cssHeader: GL chart custom properties — the token layer of the theme.
DOWNSTREAM COPY of `grammar.md`, via `tokens.json`. This file and
`src/tokens.ts` are emitted from the same source, so they cannot disagree.
The custom-property names are the ones the spec PDF itself uses (--c-1,
--c-1-dark, --ink-2, --gridline, --axis, --accent), so spec text maps to code
without translation. They are scoped to `.gl-figure` rather than `:root` so
an unprefixed name like `--accent` cannot collide with a host application's
own variables. Everything inside a figure inherits them.

$why: Prose whose code left this file. Kept here so the rationale is not lost in
the move; the emitter does not write it into either output.

doc: The nth series' tone triple, in spec order. Wraps past six — but if you are
wrapping, the chart has too many series: mute the rest and let one or two
focus series carry the finding (Decision Rule 1 + §14).

$why: The faces behind `--font-sans` and `--font-serif`, and the single owner of
that list. `scripts/emit-tokens.mjs` inlines each file as base64 into
`src/fonts.css`; `docs/build-docs.mjs` and `examples/build.mjs` read the
same list to inline the same faces into their self-contained pages.
`family` MUST equal the first entry of the stack the token declares. This is
the whole reason the block exists: declaring the face as `InterVariable`
while `--font-sans` asks for `Inter` loads 340 KB no selector can match and
drops the page to the system sans — silently, because Inter and San
Francisco are near-identical by design. TanStack then measures axis gutters
against the wrong face, so the geometry is wrong too, not just the type.
Italic Inter is deliberately absent: nothing in a figure sets sans italic.
Italic serif is NOT — `grammar.md` §2 assigns it to the chart source line,
which every figure carries.

faces.doc: Axis text, labels, legends, table cells — everything inside a figure.
The chart source line (§2), which is required on every figure.

cssHeader: GL brand faces, inlined — the type half of the theme.
import '@growth-lab/gl-charts/fonts.css';
GENERATED from `tokens.json` by `scripts/emit-tokens.mjs`. Never hand-edit.
Separate from `theme.css`, and opt-in, because it is ~1.4 MB: a host that
already serves Inter and Source Serif 4 under those exact family names
should not pay for it twice. A host that does NOT serve them must import
this, or every figure silently renders in the system sans and serif.
Each face is the VARIABLE font declared across the full `font-weight`
range, so the browser instances the real weight axis. Declaring a single
weight would make it synthesise a faux bold from the 400 master instead —
which is what `theme_gl.R` does today, and the reason a GL chart rendered
through R has no 500 or 600 in it at all.
`font-display: block` rather than `swap`: a headless screenshot or a print
render that swaps mid-layout captures the fallback metrics.

declarations.name: ink

section.title: Ink — a four-layer warm ramp
body: Warm browns, not neutral greys: the ramp sits on paper, not on a screen.

declarations.$order: JS hoists integer-like object keys, so authoring order is stated explicitly.

DEFAULT.doc: Chart title, axis line context, strong emphasis. PDF alias: --chart-title

2.doc: Axis line, axis labels, tick labels, annotations. PDF alias: --chart-axis-label / --axis

4.doc: Trendlines, deep-background markers. Rarely used outside charts.

section.title: Accent
body: `accent` and `c-1-dark` are intentionally the same hex: when the c-1 series
needs a direct label or legend mark it uses the dark tone, which clears

DEFAULT.doc: Figure label, eyebrow, accent text. PDF alias: --chart-accent

paper.doc: Content paper — pure white, so figures land neutral and color reads true.

paperWarm.doc: Warm surface — accent panels, quote tint.

rule.doc: Hairline borders between content blocks (not for in-chart use).

section.title: Categorical palette — six hues, three tones each
body: Three tones, three jobs — the most-violated rule in the spec:
main  → every fill and every line
dark  → strokes on OVERLAPPING marks, and every text element tied to the
color (direct labels, legend entries, callouts, annotations)
light → backgrounds, faded states, sequential ramp tail
The only place `dark` is used as a *fill* is the three-tone stacked area.

c-1.doc: Primary — single-series default; institutional voice. dark === accent.

declarations.name: muted
doc: De-emphasis — the "everyone else" layer in the pop-up effect (§14).
A cool grey that recedes behind the warm ink and the categorical hues.
The three-tone rule applies here too, without exception: a `muted.main`
line must have its end-label in `muted.dark`, never in `muted.main`.

declarations.name: paletteOrder
doc: Categorical hues in the order the spec requires they be spent: c-1 first,
then c-2, and so on. Using all six requires absolute necessity; needing more
than six means the representation mode should be re-thought (Decision Rule 1).

declarations.name: categoricalMains
declarations.doc: Main tones only, in spec order — the default discrete fill scale.

section.title: Sequential ramps — ordered encodings, no midpoint
body: Darker = higher, always. Five steps by default; three for a coarse
classification, seven or more for a fine gradient.

declarations.name: defaultSequential
declarations.doc: Default ramp unless the variable carries a hue convention (heat, vegetation).

section.title: Diverging ramps — meaningful midpoints only
body: The boundary between the two hues IS the midpoint. Six steps by default.
Never use a diverging ramp on a purely positive scale — readers will read
midpoint meaning into the boundary that isn't there.

div-3-1.doc: teal ↔ blue — loss vs. gain within one family.

section.title: Typography
body: Two families, two jobs. Serif for the title and the source line; sans for
everything else in the figure. No third family. No monospace, ever —
numerals are Inter with tabular figures.

serif.doc: Chart title and chart source (italic). Nothing else in the figure block.

sans.doc: Subtitles, axis labels, ticks, series labels, annotations, legends.

declarations.name: minTextSize
doc: 12px is the FLOOR for all in-chart text. Labels that do not fit at 12px are
dropped, never shrunk below it.

figureLabel.doc: "FIGURE 4" — top of every figure block, numbered sequentially.

title.doc: The headline. ALWAYS ends in a period — it reads as a finding, not a label.

subtitle.doc: Units, period, unit of analysis. Omit when redundant with the title. No period.

source.doc: Always required. One line below the chart. Italic serif marks provenance.

axisLabel.doc: Names the dimension and its units. Sentence case — never all caps.

axisTick.doc: Numeric values along each axis. Tabular figures so digits align.

doc: Direct label at a line end, or a legend entry. Color is NOT set here —
it is always the DARK tone of the series it names (Decision Rule 2).

color.comment: placeholder — override per series with its dark tone

tickLabelOffset.doc: Tick label sits 6px outside the axis.

doc: Axis-label offset is measured from the START of the tick label, not from
the axis line — 20px left of the leftmost character of the widest Y tick
label, and 20px below the X tick baseline. Measuring from the axis line
lets wide ticks like "250" collide with the rotated Y label.

lineWidthFocus.doc: The highlighted focus series — 1.2x thicker, not a 2x jump.

pointRadius.doc: Scatter circle: spec allows 5–7px; 6 is the default.

doc: 1px gap between stacked BAR segments — gives the category boundary a clean
edge and helps readers with low color discrimination separate bands.
Stacked *areas* sit edge-to-edge with no gap (the lightness step separates).
Treemap tiles are separated by a PAPER GUTTER, never by a stroke, at every
depth — including a flat single-level treemap (`SPEC.md` §3.4.1).
Measured off the spec's own plates: Figures 4 (p.17) and 11 (p.24) both run
a uniform 4.8px channel on both axes, rounded to 5 here. Figure 11 is why
the flat case needs it too — its seven supporting tiles are all `c-muted`,
and the gutter is the only thing that keeps them from reading as one grey
mass. Blocks get double, which is what "thicker" meant when the rule was
still written as a paper border.

treemapLabelPad.doc: Inset from a treemap tile's top-left corner to its label block.

doc: Baseline of a tile's name line, below the tile's top edge, and the step
down to the `value · share` line.

labelHalo.doc: Halo radius on direct labels drawn over data, so they stay legible.

doc: Dash pattern for a REFERENCE rule — a threshold, target or identity line
(§3.4.2). Chrome, not data: it also takes `ink-3` at gridline weight, so
nothing about it can be mistaken for a series. §3.4 keeps data lines
solid, which is what makes the dash readable as "not a measurement".
An error-bar cap or rug tick — TWICE the 4px axis tick, so a tick that
carries a value cannot be read as axis chrome. Width stays `tickWidth`.
Arrowhead on a directed-change mark. Fixed pixels, never scaled: the
head says *direction*, and a head that grew with the magnitude would
encode the value twice.
Arrowhead on a field vector — smaller than a change arrow's, because a
field is hundreds of marks and the 8px head fills the plot.

bandPadding.doc: Gap between categorical bars, as a fraction of the band.

doc: Padding on a POINT scale — lines or dots over discrete categories. Lower
than the bar padding because it only has to keep the end marks off the
axis, not separate adjacent marks.
Padding on a BINNED axis — histogram, matrix heatmap, calendar,
Marimekko. Zero, and not negotiable: bins partition a continuum, so they
must abut. A gap invents a discreteness the data does not have.
Separation between bins is `binGap`, which is chrome over the boundary
rather than padding in the scale (§3.4.3).
Paper channel between adjacent histogram bins, in px. One hue abutting
itself reads as a single mass — the failure §3.4.1 names for a one-hue
treemap — so a bin takes a separator on the same principle as the 1px
the stacked bar leaves between segments.
FIXED px, not a fraction of the band: `binPadding` stays zero so the
band still spans the full bin, and a proportional gap would widen as the
bin count fell while the data said nothing.
Cut as `binGap / 2` of INSET per side, never as a stroke. A centred
paper stroke also runs along the top of the rect and would erase the
1–2px bars in the tail of a skewed distribution — which is the finding.
No CSS custom property: unlike `stackGap`, which patch.css needs as a
stroke-width, this one is consumed only as a mark option in TypeScript.
Inner radius of a donut as a fraction of the outer — big enough to hold
a centred total at the 12px type floor (§3.8).
Paper gap between adjacent arcs, in px at the outer radius. The same 1px
the stacked bar leaves between segments — an arc IS a stacked bar bent
round, so the separation rule should not change with the coordinate
system.
The legend mark's box — the side of a square swatch and the diameter of
a dot (§3.11). One box for every mark kind so the labels beside them
share a baseline no matter what the series is drawn as.
A line series' legend mark is a RULE, not a square (§3.11), and it has
to be long enough to read as a line and to show a dash pattern — 16px
holds two cycles of `ruleDash`. Its stroke is the series' own:
`lineWidth`, or `lineWidthFocus` where that series is the focus.
Stroke on the square that stands for a RADAR POLYGON (§3.11) — the
polygon has a fill and a stroke, so its miniature carries both.
Matches `radarStrokeWidth` less the shrink to 10px. A band takes no
stroke at all (§3.4), so this does not apply to one.

legendMarkGap.doc: Gap between a legend mark and its label (§3.11).

doc: Gap between entries in a horizontal legend. Wide enough that a mark
binds to the label on its RIGHT and not to the one before it.
How far an annotation stands off the EDGE of the mark it names —
a bubble's radius, a bar's cap, an arrowhead's tip (§3.12).
Measured from the rendered edge, never from the mark's anchor point.
A fixed offset from the anchor lands inside the mark the moment the
radius becomes a size channel, which is exactly what a bubble chart
is.

grammar.match: clears the edge of the mark it names by **8px**

doc: The leader that connects an annotation to its mark when no side is
clear (§3.12). 1px in the mark's dark tone, no arrowhead — it is a
pointer, not a vector.

declarations.name: opacity
doc: The 0.8 rule is for OVERLAP. Scatter circles use the same 0.8 on fill and
stroke so overlapping points darken together into a density signal.
Single-layer marks (bars, treemap tiles, choropleths) stay at full opacity —
overlap isn't a risk there and lowering opacity just dilutes the color.

overlap.doc: Scatter circles, overlaid polygons — fill AND stroke together.

grammar.match: The 0.8 rule is for overlapping marks

full.doc: Bars, areas, treemap tiles, choropleth polygons, lines.

radarFill.doc: Radar polygon fill — lower, so gridlines and axis labels read through.

comment: The spec PDF's in-chart aliases. Same values, spec-local names.

sections.comment: Categorical — six hues, three tones each

comment: main = fills + lines · dark = strokes on overlap + ALL tied text
· light = backgrounds, faded states, sequential tail
De-emphasis — the "everyone else" layer of the pop-up effect.
`defaultChartTheme.palette` is six `var(--ts-chart-N, <hex>)` strings, so
redefining these six names re-skins any TanStack chart with no rebuild of
the definition. Mapping them to the GL main tones means even a chart built
with a bare `defineChart()` — no GL preset — lands on the GL palette.
`glTheme` (src/chart.ts) sets the same values on the definition; belt and
braces, because Canvas-rendered charts cannot see CSS variables.
Label halo and focus fill default to the `Canvas` system color; on GL
paper they must be the paper white.
12px is the floor for every piece of in-chart text.
Chrome vs. data (§3.4.2): a reference rule is dashed ink-3 at gridline
weight; a stem, connector, tick or arrow carries the series tone and
the line weight. Same geometry, opposite jobs.
Categorical axis padding — bars, points, and bins (§3.5).
Legend and annotation geometry (§3.11, §3.12). The legend mark is a
miniature of the mark it names, so its box is chrome the figure
block draws itself — unlike everything above it, which TanStack
draws and reads from the theme object instead.

$why: `check-tokens.mjs --downstream` scans these for GL hexes and reports drift.
Report-only: it never fails a build, because the repo hand-carries these
values and we do not yet know the set is clean.
`documented` mirrors README.md's "Where each value lives downstream" table.
`undocumented` are files that demonstrably carry GL hexes but are missing
from that table — the incomplete propagation map is itself the finding.
`docs/nil/` (upstream) and `playground/` (derived) are out of scope per
README.md.

documented.carries: R: the `gl` token list, palettes, `save_fig` sizes, geom defaults
xelatex: font families + the color palette (R Markdown PDF route)
Python constants → gl.docx / gl.dotx (px→pt compromises documented in-file)
Web/SVG: typed token module (GENERATED from this file)
Web/SVG: CSS custom properties, scoped to .gl-figure (GENERATED from this file)

undocumented.carries: GL_HEX allowlist (~30 hexes) — a new token false-positives until added here
Lua constants, OOXML no-# uppercase hex
condensed chart spec: palette + geometry tables
inline :root vars for the eval index page

$why: Documented non-token colors that must not be reported as drift.
`externalPalettes` is a directory of CSVs: the Atlas HS / SITC sector
palettes and colour scales are an external standard that overrides the
categorical palette for product data (grammar.md "Sector-specific
palettes"), so the R theme and the linter legitimately carry them.
`grammarTokens` are grammar.md colours outside the chart medium — the
cover paper and the cover pattern artwork.
